prompt: [Sentence Completion] Desmond's locker was a monument to -------: crumpled worksheets spilled from the top shelf, a single sneaker lay on its side with no partner in sight, and three overdue library books were wedged beneath a broken umbrella.
explanation: The list of crumpled papers, a lost sneaker, overdue books and a broken umbrella describes a state of total disorder: disarray.
distractor_rationales: bravado — a locker of crumpled, lost and broken things shows no boastful display of courage.
urbanity — crumpled papers, a lost shoe and a broken umbrella are the opposite of refined polish.
finesse — 'spilled', 'wedged' and 'broken' describe the opposite of skilled, delicate handling.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The violinist's vibrato was so ------- that it never drew attention to itself; listeners noticed only that each long, steady note seemed to glow from within.
explanation: 'So ... that it never drew attention to itself' calls for a quality so delicate it goes unnoticed: subtle.
distractor_rationales: grating — a harsh, irritating sound would draw attention, which the sentence says it never did.
spasmodic — fits-and-starts vibrato would draw attention and could not make each note sound 'steady.'
staccato — short, clipped playing contradicts 'each long, steady note.'

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Coach Ibarra's training rules were openly -------: two practices a day in the August heat, sprints until someone collapsed, and no water break for anyone until the drill had been run without a single mistake.
explanation: Withholding water until a drill is perfect and running sprints until collapse are examples of harsh, severe rules: draconian.
distractor_rationales: slapdash — 'without a single mistake' shows the rules demanded precision, not careless haste.
whimsical — a fixed schedule of two daily practices and set conditions is not playful or fanciful.
covert — the rules were 'openly' imposed, so they were not secret.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The band's new drummer was not merely punctual but so ------- that he arrived an hour before every rehearsal to tune the kit, tape down loose cables, and check that each microphone stand was the right height.
explanation: 'Not merely punctual but so ... that' asks for a stronger form of reliability; arriving early to carefully prepare everything shows he is conscientious.
distractor_rationales: gregarious — he spends the hour on equipment, not socializing with anyone.
impetuous — an hour of methodical preparation is the opposite of rash, hasty action.
sardonic — nothing he does is mocking; the sentence lists only careful tasks.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The new office manager's emails were famously -------: each one ran to several paragraphs, restated in full the question it was answering, and closed with a summary of points he had already made twice.
explanation: Several paragraphs per email, the question restated in full, and a closing summary of points already made twice describe emails of great length: voluminous.
distractor_rationales: inscrutable — restating the question and summarizing make the emails easy to follow, not impossible to understand.
obsequious — nothing in the list flatters the reader; the emails are only long and repetitive.
undiplomatic — the details concern length and repetition, not rudeness or tactlessness.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Lucia, who later said she had enjoyed the evening, was nonetheless so ------- at her cousin's crowded wedding that she spent most of the reception reading quietly in the coat room, slipping away whenever a guest tried to start a conversation.
explanation: Enjoying the night yet avoiding conversation and retreating to a quiet room shows someone drained by crowds and inclined inward: introverted.
distractor_rationales: vainglorious — a boastful person would want an audience, not hide in the coat room.
sycophantic — a flatterer would seek out guests to please them, not slip away whenever one approached.
punctilious — nothing concerns strict attention to etiquette; leaving guests mid-conversation is the reverse of it.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Visitors to the gallery found the sculpture thoroughly -------: a bronze horse balanced on one hoof atop a marble egg, a rusted bicycle wheel spun slowly above its head, and a recording of goose calls played from somewhere inside the base.
explanation: A horse on an egg, a bicycle wheel and goose calls are mismatched elements that do not belong together: incongruous.
distractor_rationales: spartan — three clashing, crowded elements are the opposite of plain and bare.
imitative — the sentence gives no model or earlier work it copies; it describes oddness, not borrowing.
evanescent — bronze, marble and a rusted wheel are permanent materials, not fleeting ones.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The chemistry final was so ------- that not one student finished it in the time allowed, and even Mr. Osei, who wrote it, needed the full ninety minutes to work through his own answer key.
explanation: 'So ... that' no one finished and even its author needed ninety minutes means it was extremely demanding: taxing.
distractor_rationales: superficial — a shallow test would not take its own author the full ninety minutes.
slanted — nothing suggests the exam favoured some students; it defeated every student equally.
forgiving — an exam nobody could finish was not easy on students.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The poet's notebooks show just how ------- she was with her own work: she might rewrite a single line forty times over a month, read each version aloud to her sister to test its rhythm, and still strike it from the final draft.
explanation: Forty rewrites, testing each aloud and still cutting the line show she held her own work to a harsh, demanding standard and let nothing pass: unsparing.
distractor_rationales: impulsive — a month of deliberate revision is the opposite of acting on sudden whim.
slipshod — forty careful rewrites rule out careless, sloppy work.
sanguine — striking the line after forty tries shows she was never confident or easily satisfied with it.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The goalkeeper was so ------- that, after diving the wrong way on a penalty kick, she twisted back in midair and tipped the ball over the crossbar with her trailing foot.
explanation: 'So ... that' she could twist back in midair and reach with her trailing foot shows unusual flexibility: limber.
distractor_rationales: stoic — calmly enduring hardship would not let her change direction in midair; the clue is physical, not emotional.
burly — bulk and heaviness work against twisting in midair.
sullen — a resentful, gloomy mood says nothing about twisting in midair; the clue is physical, not emotional.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Teo's grandfather is cheerfully -------: he reuses each tea bag three times, darns his socks rather than buy new ones, and will drive across town to save four cents a gallon on gas.
explanation: Reusing tea bags, darning socks and chasing four cents of savings are examples of extreme reluctance to spend: miserly.
distractor_rationales: melancholic — he is described as 'cheerfully' so, not as gloomy.
standoffish — every detail concerns money, not coldness toward other people.
impudent — nothing he does is disrespectful or cheeky toward anyone.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] So ------- was the actor's portrayal of the aging king that several audience members, forgetting they were in a theater, called out to warn him of his daughter's betrayal.
explanation: 'So ... that' the audience forgot they were in a theater requires a performance that seemed entirely real: convincing.
distractor_rationales: bombastic — overblown, inflated acting would remind viewers they were watching a show.
perfunctory — a half-hearted performance would not absorb the audience enough to call out.
irreverent — mocking the role would break the illusion rather than make spectators treat the king as real.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Ms. Achebe's managing style was plainly -------: she approved every purchase over five dollars herself, rewrote her staff's memos before they could be sent, and demanded hourly updates on projects meant to take months.
explanation: Approving every small purchase, rewriting others' memos and demanding hourly updates are examples of controlling others: domineering.
distractor_rationales: magnanimous — nothing in the list is generous or forgiving; she trusts her staff with nothing.
mercurial — she does the same thing every time (every purchase, every memo, every hour), so she is not unpredictable.
curt — the details concern control over others' work, not short or brusque speech.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Jonah was hardly ------- about his science fair project; he chose a topic the night before it was due, and his entire display was one poster board labeled in pencil.
explanation: 'Hardly' signals the opposite of what he showed; choosing a topic the night before and making one pencil poster shows little effort, so he was hardly industrious.
distractor_rationales: incredulous — the sentence describes how little work he did, not any disbelief.
indignant — nothing shows anger or a sense of being wronged.
mawkish — sentimental gushing has no connection to a rushed, last-minute display.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The band's new album is decidedly -------: it opens with a sea shanty, moves through a slow jazz ballad and two thrash-metal tracks, and closes with a lullaby sung entirely in Welsh.
explanation: A shanty, jazz, thrash metal and a Welsh lullaby are examples of drawing on many different styles: eclectic.
distractor_rationales: morbid — a lullaby and a sea shanty are not preoccupied with death or gloom.
listless — two thrash-metal tracks rule out an energy-less album.
raucous — a slow ballad and a lullaby rule out loud, rowdy throughout.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The retired umpire's memoir is so ------- that he admits to every call he got wrong, names the managers he could not stand, and even confesses that he once dozed off in the bullpen during a rain delay.
explanation: 'So ... that' he admits his mistakes, names people he disliked and confesses embarrassing moments shows direct honesty: forthright.
distractor_rationales: flowery — the sentence concerns what he admits, not ornamental language.
maudlin — the confessions are plain admissions, including a comic one, not tearful sentimentality.
pedantic — he is owning up to errors, not fussing over minor rules or showing off learning.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] At the student council debate Farid was shamelessly -------: he answered every question by praising whoever had asked it, agreed with whichever candidate had spoken last, and promised the lunch line a soda fountain he had no way to deliver.
explanation: Praising questioners, agreeing with everyone and making crowd-pleasing promises are examples of trying to win favour: ingratiating.
distractor_rationales: uncouth — he flatters every questioner, which is smooth crowd-pleasing, not crude or ill-mannered behaviour.
scathing — he praises whoever asks and agrees with everyone, so he is not harshly critical.
circumspect — promising a soda fountain he could not deliver is careless, not cautious.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Even the head chef, who praised almost nothing, called the new line cook's knife work so ------- that, though he worked slowly, every slice of carrot came out exactly as thick as the one before it.
explanation: 'So ... that' every slice came out exactly the same thickness shows precise, error-free cutting: accurate.
distractor_rationales: brisk — 'though he worked slowly' rules out quick, energetic work.
theatrical — the praise is for identical slices, not for showy flourishes.
skittish — nervous, jumpy cutting would produce uneven slices, not exactly matching ones.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The art teacher's warm-up exercise was decidedly -------: draw with only the hand you do not write with, keep your eyes closed for the first five minutes, and sketch a classmate's face without once lifting the pencil from the page.
explanation: Drawing with the wrong hand, eyes closed and without lifting the pencil are examples of departing from usual methods: unorthodox.
distractor_rationales: nebulous — the three rules are specific and clear, not vague.
indulgent — strict rules on hand, eyes and pencil are demanding, not permissive.
contradictory — none of the three rules conflicts with another; all can be followed at once.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The aging pitcher was not merely ------- about his slump but downright cheerful, joking with reporters that his fastball had finally slowed to a speed his grandmother could hit.
explanation: 'Not merely X but downright cheerful' requires a milder version of good humour; calm and untroubled fits: unruffled.
distractor_rationales: waspish — sharp, irritable remarks contradict 'downright cheerful.'
vengeful — joking at his own expense shows no wish to pay anyone back.
defiant — he openly admits his fastball has slowed rather than refusing to accept it.
